product_scope.problem_statement: The system must orchestrate massive daily API calls over a large and growing record base while preserving per-provider isolation, resilience, and durable result storage.
product_scope.goal: Provide a serverless solution on AWS that schedules, dispatches, executes, retries, and persists provider API calls in a controlled and scalable way.
success_outcomes: Daily pending records are dispatched without creating a thundering herd at provider endpoints.
Calls for the same provider are processed strictly one at a time and in order.
Transient and terminal failures are distinguished and handled differently.
Execution results and terminal failures are persisted for later audit and analysis.
The solution can scale from an initial dataset of 1 million records to higher volumes without requiring a monolithic batch process.

in_scope: Daily orchestration of pending records for provider API execution.
Temporal distribution of workload to reduce peak traffic concentration.
Queue-based decoupling between record selection and provider API execution.
Persistence of successful results and terminal failures.
Classification of retryable and non-retryable provider errors.
Operational support for retries, dead-letter handling, and auditability.
Infrastructure definition as code for the required AWS resources.
A code structure that preserves separation between domain logic and AWS-specific adapters.
Automated tests for core business behavior.
out_of_scope: A full business UI or operator dashboard.
Provider-specific payload transformation rules beyond a generic request contract.
Manual operations tooling for replay, backfill, or record repair beyond basic support hooks.
Cost optimization to final production thresholds.
Advanced analytics or BI over stored results.
A full production-ready security and compliance program beyond reasonable technical defaults.

actors.name: Scheduler
actors.description: Triggers the start of the daily orchestration window.

actors.name: Orchestration System
actors.description: Selects pending records, dispatches work, coordinates execution, and routes failures.

actors.name: Provider API
actors.description: External or internal endpoint that receives one request per record.

actors.name: Technical Reviewer
actors.description: Evaluates whether the implementation satisfies the challenge requirements and architectural rationale.

user_journeys.name: Daily scheduled execution
steps: A daily trigger starts the orchestration flow for the target date.
The system selects pending records associated with that execution window.
The system dispatches records into an execution queue using provider-aware grouping.
The system executes provider calls while respecting one-at-a-time processing per provider.
Successful executions are persisted as results.

user_journeys.name: Transient failure recovery
steps: A provider call fails with a retryable error.
The system identifies the failure as transient.
The system retries according to an orchestration policy.
If a retry eventually succeeds, the final successful result is persisted.
If retries are exhausted, the work item is moved to an operational failure path.

user_journeys.name: Terminal failure audit trail
steps: A provider call fails with a non-retryable error.
The system identifies the failure as terminal.
The system persists the failure outcome with enough context for audit.
The failed item stops retrying and is routed to a final failure outcome.

user_journeys.name: High-volume execution without a monolithic scan-and-process bottleneck
steps: The system is asked to process a large pending dataset.
The orchestration flow breaks the work into manageable units instead of relying on one long-running function to handle everything.
Independent work units progress in parallel where safe.
Provider-level serialization remains intact even under high overall throughput.

use_cases.title: Dispatch pending records for a target date
use_cases.description: The system gathers eligible records for a scheduled date and enqueues them for downstream execution.

use_cases.title: Enforce provider-level execution isolation
use_cases.description: The system ensures that requests for the same provider never execute concurrently and preserve ordering.

use_cases.title: Persist successful API outcomes
use_cases.description: The system stores response metadata and payload for completed provider calls.

use_cases.title: Retry transient provider failures
use_cases.description: The system retries only failures classified as temporary or safe to repeat.

use_cases.title: Persist and isolate terminal failures
use_cases.description: The system stores definitive failures and prevents endless retry loops.

use_cases.title: Support operational review of failed work
use_cases.description: The system leaves a traceable path for messages or executions that could not be completed automatically.

business_rules.rule: A pending record represents one provider API call to be executed once for its scheduled date.
Records belonging to the same provider must be processed strictly in order and never concurrently.
Records belonging to different providers may be processed in parallel.
The system must distribute daily execution over time to avoid concentrated load spikes.
Retryable and non-retryable provider failures must be classified differently because they lead to different outcomes.
A terminal failure must be persisted as an auditable outcome.
The orchestration flow must remain effective for datasets starting at 1 million records and growing beyond that baseline.
The solution must avoid relying on a single linear execution that becomes a timeout or throughput bottleneck.
Stored data may include transient operational records with expiration semantics and durable result records with retention semantics.
The system must preserve enough execution evidence for technical review and operational debugging.

functional_requirements.title: Daily scheduling
functional_requirements.statement: The system must support an automated daily trigger for orchestration.

functional_requirements.title: Target-date execution
functional_requirements.statement: The system must support selecting the logical execution date for pending work.

functional_requirements.title: Massive record dispatch
functional_requirements.statement: The system must dispatch large batches of pending records without depending on one monolithic processing pass.

functional_requirements.title: Per-provider serialization
functional_requirements.statement: The system must serialize execution for each provider while allowing horizontal scaling across providers.

functional_requirements.title: Successful result persistence
functional_requirements.statement: The system must persist successful provider call outcomes.

functional_requirements.title: Transient retry handling
functional_requirements.statement: The system must retry transient failures according to an orchestration policy.

functional_requirements.title: Terminal failure handling
functional_requirements.statement: The system must stop retrying terminal failures and persist them for audit.

functional_requirements.title: Dead-letter or terminal isolation path
functional_requirements.statement: The system must isolate work items that cannot be completed automatically after the allowed retry policy.

functional_requirements.title: Time-based cleanup
functional_requirements.statement: The system must support expiration of transient data where retention is not indefinite.

functional_requirements.title: Traceability for review
functional_requirements.statement: The system must expose enough observable behavior and persisted evidence to explain what happened to a record.

interaction_expectations.expectation: The orchestration should behave deterministically from the standpoint of provider ordering even when many providers are processed at once.
Operational outcomes should be understandable through logs, persisted records, and failure paths without needing to inspect ambiguous runtime state.
The implementation should be explainable in a technical challenge setting with clear mapping from requirement to component behavior.

acceptance_criteria.given: There are pending records for a scheduled date
acceptance_criteria.then: The system dispatches those records for execution without requiring a single long-running batch process to complete the entire workload.

acceptance_criteria.given: Two or more records belong to the same provider
acceptance_criteria.then: The system processes them one at a time and in order.
It may process them in parallel without violating provider-level isolation.
The response outcome is persisted with enough data for later audit.

acceptance_criteria.given: A provider call fails with a retryable error
acceptance_criteria.when: The system classifies the error as transient
acceptance_criteria.then: The system retries the execution according to policy before declaring final failure.

acceptance_criteria.given: A provider call fails with a non-retryable error
acceptance_criteria.when: The system classifies the error as terminal
acceptance_criteria.then: The system persists the failure and stops retrying that work item.

acceptance_criteria.given: A work item cannot be completed automatically after the allowed attempts
acceptance_criteria.then: The item is isolated into a final failure path for operational review.
The architecture remains decomposed into scalable units and does not depend on a single Lambda reading and processing all records sequentially.
The workload start is distributed in a way that reduces concentrated spikes against downstream providers.

acceptance_criteria.given: A technical reviewer inspects the solution
acceptance_criteria.when: They review the repository and architecture
acceptance_criteria.then: They can trace each major challenge requirement to a specific behavior, component, or persisted outcome.

assumptions: The challenge is primarily evaluated on architecture quality, correctness of orchestration behavior, and defendable tradeoffs rather than on a complete production platform.
A generic provider request contract is sufficient for the challenge unless provider-specific rules emerge later.
A single AWS account and region are acceptable for the challenge deliverable.
The current repository structure in TypeScript and AWS CDK is the intended implementation base.
Observability and operational evidence are required at a practical challenge level, even if not all production dashboards are built.

open_questions.question: Is shuffle-sharding a mandatory deliverable for challenge acceptance or a stretch goal that can be addressed after core provider serialization is fully correct?
How much of the large-scale ingestion strategy must be fully implemented versus explicitly documented and partially scaffolded for the challenge?
Does challenge acceptance require explicit idempotency persistence beyond FIFO deduplication and retry-safe design?
